problem: Prior VLN-CE training (Krantz et al. 2020's CMA) supervises the agent, both in teacher forcing and in DAgger, with the best action along the shortest path to the goal. When the agent drifts off the reference path, this goal-aligned signal can contradict the instruction. Existing metrics (SR, SPL, nDTW) also do not directly measure how many instructed waypoints or sub-instructions the agent actually follows.
motivation: The path an instruction describes can differ from the shortest path to the goal: about 6% of VLN-CE R2R episodes have nDTW(shortest, reference) < 0.8. The mismatch matters most in 'off the path' states. Continuous episodes are long (55.88 steps on average vs 4-6 nodes in discrete VLN), so a dense per-step signal pulling the agent back to the instructed path should help. The paper builds on Jain et al. (2019), whose sparse, episode-end fidelity reward via policy gradient is harder to optimize.
key_idea: Replace the goal-oriented oracle action with a language-aligned one: at every step, supervise the agent (cross-entropy, in both teacher forcing and DAgger) with the shortest-path action toward the nearest waypoint on the instruction's reference path, instead of toward the goal.
insight: Changing only the supervision target consistently improves both goal reaching and instruction fidelity on R2R-CE val. Val-unseen: SR 0.29→0.35, nDTW 0.50→0.54, WA 0.41→0.47. The gain is concentrated on episodes whose reference path diverges from the shortest path (the low-nDTW bins in Fig. 3). Waypoint density barely matters: #2, #4, pano, #15 and step all give val-unseen SR 0.32–0.35, which the authors attribute to short R2R paths (~10 m) where one sub-instruction spans several pano nodes. Mixing goal and language losses in DAgger (L only, L+G, random L/G) always underperforms pure LAW pano; L+G drops val-unseen SR to 0.27, so the goal signal actively conflicts with instruction following.
method: Base policy: the Cross-Modal Attention (CMA) model from VLN-CE. RGB goes through an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 and depth through a DD-PPO PointNav-pretrained ResNet-50. Instructions use GloVe embeddings and a BiLSTM (BERT features for RxR). One GRU tracks state history and drives instruction and visual attention; a second GRU predicts the action.

Language-aligned action sensor: the oracle action is a* = g(x_t, φ(x_t, W)). φ picks the reference-path waypoint nearest to the agent's 3D position x_t, and g returns the best shortest-path action toward that waypoint. This replaces the goal-oriented shortest-path sensor.

Training: the VLN-CE two-stage regime with LAW supervision in both stages. Stage 1 is teacher-forcing behavior cloning on ~150k EnvDrop-augmented trajectories (~60 h). Stage 2 is DAgger fine-tuning on the 4475 original trajectories (~36 h on 2 V100s), with a per-step cross-entropy loss.

Waypoint-density variants: goal only (LAW#1); LAW#2, #4 and #15 (equidistant samples on the reference path); LAW pano (R2R nav-graph nodes, avg ~6, ~2 m apart); LAW step (dense 0.25 m reference-path points).

Waypoint Accuracy (WA) metric: the fraction of reference waypoints the agent passes within 0.5 m. Combined with FG-R2R sub-instruction-to-sub-path mappings, it gives an interpretable count of sub-instructions completed.

setting.backbone: CMA (ResNet-50 RGB [ImageNet] + ResNet-50 depth [DD-PPO] + GloVe/BiLSTM instruction encoder + 2 GRUs), trained with IL; BERT instruction features for the RxR variant
setting.training_data: VLN-CE R2R train (4475 trajectories) plus ~150k EnvDrop augmented trajectories ported to VLN-CE for teacher forcing, then DAgger on the original trajectories. RxR experiments: RxR-Habitat English split, teacher forcing only.
setting.action_space: low-level FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN LEFT/RIGHT 15° / STOP
setting.privileged: none at test time (ground-truth reference-path waypoints used only for training supervision)

numbers_note: All metrics except TL and NE are printed as fractions (e.g. 0.35) and converted here to 0-100. The R2R-CE test split reports only TL, NE, OS, SR and SPL because the leaderboard gives no nDTW or SDTW. RxR-CE results are on the English split only, with teacher forcing only. The nDTW-binned analysis (Fig. 3) and the finding that LAW#4 beats LAW pano on paths definable by 4 waypoints are shown only in figures. The other density variants (#2, #4, #15) and the goal/language loss-mixing variants are in tables but omitted here.
results: On R2R-CE, LAW pano beats the same CMA model with goal-oriented supervision on every metric. Val-unseen: SR 0.35 vs 0.29, SPL 0.31 vs 0.27, nDTW 0.54 vs 0.50, WA 0.47 vs 0.41. Val-seen: SR 0.40 vs 0.34, WA 0.56 vs 0.48. On the test leaderboard SR and SPL are tied (0.28/0.25), and only OS improves (0.38 vs 0.36). On RxR-CE English val-unseen, LAW step improves nDTW 0.36→0.38 and WA 0.27→0.33, and LAW pano raises SR 0.06→0.10.
limitations: Gains do not transfer to the R2R-CE test split in SR or SPL (tied with the goal baseline); instruction-fidelity metrics could not be evaluated there.
Only one architecture (CMA) with absolute performance well below later waypoint-based VLN-CE methods; the density ablation is inconclusive, with all variants performing similarly.
The RxR experiments use only the English split, teacher-forcing only, and yield very low absolute SR (~0.1).
builds_on: Stay on the Path / CLS fidelity reward (Jain et al. 2019)
compares_to: Mixed goal + language loss variants (L only, L+G, random L/G)
